messages.subject: hazard-rate detection function parameter estimations
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

A friend of mine asked me this question and I didn't know the answer and
could find one either.  I thought some of you may be able to help us.

The question is how does DISTANCE estimate the parameters for the
hazard-rate detection function.  Buckland (1985) reported that "...
encountered convergence problems when attempting to estimate the parameters
of this model (hazard rate model) using maximum likelihood estimation on
ungrouped data.  A computer program to implement the method on grouped data
is available from the author."  I briefly looked at the Distance sampling
book, but I could not find any relevant material.  I tried help files in
DISTANCE with no success.

I hope someone can direct me to the right directions!!

Thanks!

Tomo

Reference:
Buckland, S. T. 1985. Perpendicular distance models for line transect
sampling. Biometrics 41: 177-195.

********************************************************
Tomoharu Eguchi
Department of Ecology
310 Lewis Hall
Montana State University
Bozeman, MT 59717
(406) 994-1769
egu...@montana.edu
http://www.esg.montana.edu/eguchi

messages.subject: Re: hazard-rate detection function parameter estimations
messages.body_plain:
> > The question is how does DISTANCE estimate the parameters for the
> > hazard-rate detection function.  Buckland (1985) reported that "...
> > encountered convergence problems when attempting to estimate the parameters
> > of this model (hazard rate model) using maximum likelihood estimation on
> > ungrouped data.  A computer program to implement the method on grouped data
> > is available from the author."  I briefly looked at the Distance sampling
> > book, but I could not find any relevant material.  I tried help files in
> > DISTANCE with no success.

Distance does maximize the likelihood for both grouped and ungrouped
data.  A reparameterization was used which substantially reduces
the correlation in the parameter estimates, and convergence is now seldom
a problem, at least for the case that no adjustment terms are added to
the hazard-rate fit.  Thus Distance uses the parameterization given in the
1993 book, not the 1985 paper.

i.e. g(y)=1-exp[-(y/a)^{-b}]

The hazard-rate model can fit implausible shapes, in which detection
probability falls rapidly with increasing distance from the line,
if your data are particularly spiked.  The constraint b>1 reduces this
problem.  This constraint can be set in Distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Help on using distance
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am doing a one-year population survey of N. American songbirds in
Connecticut and am using Distance to determine density/abundance etc.
However, I've found the data explorer to be a little frustrating and the
Help provided with the program doesn't seem to answer my questions. ( For
instance what exactly do they require for the "survey effort" values? Is
this the number of points within a habitat, the number of times each point
is visited? etc.  How can the data be entered in order to allow for density
values to be calculated by month and species?)
  Are there additional guides, aids or references where I can find the
answers to such questions?

Thank-you,

Vanessa Parker-Geisman

Vanessa.pa...@mail.trincoll.edu

messages.subject: Re: Help on using distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vanessa,

I'm replying to the list as my reply contains some general points.

I'm sorry you are not finding the information you need in the online help.
So far as I know, there aren't any additional guides, etc out there, although
someone may have written something (anyone else on the list know of
anything?).  I have it in mind one of these days to write a short, tutorial-
based pamplet along the lines of "An Introduction to Distance", but have not
found the time yet.

Meanwhile, the only other source of help is the archives of this list - you
can Search for keywords on via the web interface at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html

For example, I found the following messages, which are relevant to your
questions (particularly the first 2):

000020 99/01/20 11:12 329  problems with data file structuring
000021 99/01/22 01:05 224  Re: problems with data file structuring
000058 99/08/02 18:57 80  QUERY: Multi-species design in Distance
000204 01/01/22 09:31 70  Re: Multiple counts of a single transect

There are probably more there - I only did a quick search.

Of course there is always the Distance Sampling book (available online), but
that does not contain information about the program, only the methods behind
the program.

Now, to address your questions.  It sounds like your study design may be more
complex than Distance 3.5 can deal with in one project or run.  You don't
give details, but it sounds like you have multiple points located in
different habitats, and that you visited each point once a month for a year,
surveying for multiple species.  Sounds like you are interested in estimating
density by month for each species.

When the time periods are close together, so that the population can be
considered "closed", and you are only interested in estimating density over
the whole time period, then you can pool the data from multiple visits to the
same point.  In this case, the sample data layer would contain one record for
each point, and the "survey effort" is the number of visits to each point.
For multi-species studies you could either have a separate project file for
each species, or you could have a field in the observation layer for species,
and use the data selection tab of the Data Filter to pick out only the
species you are interested in for each analysis.

When the time periods are not close together and you are interested in the
change over time, then you can enter time period as a stratum (month, in your
case) and do a stratified analysis.  In this case, the survey effort will be
the number of times the point was visited per time period (month) -- often
only once.  There is one problem to do with estimating variance, because your
repeats of the same points are not independant replicates -- I cover this in
the message
000021 99/01/22 01:05 224  Re: problems with data file structuring
in the archives.

Another problem in your case is that you already have a stratum - habitat -
and Distance 3.5 can only deal with one level of stratification at once.  If
you have a lot of data, then you could have one project file for each month,
and analyze them all separately.  However, most people don't have the luxury
of that much data (especially for the rarer species in multi-species studies)
and would like to look at the possibility of combining data from the
different time periods and/or habitats for estimating the detection function.
(This is commonly done by trying a pooled analysis and recording the AIC,
then separate analyses for each time period and summing the AICs -- if the
"by time period" analysis has a lower AIC then it is preferred.)  In this
case you won't be able to get away from doing some of the calculations for
estimating density by hand -- see section 3.8.1 of the book and the example
8.5.  Probably your best bet for setting up a project file for such analysis
is to have month as an extra field in the observation layer.  Then, you can
easily do the all data analysis, and use the data filter to select out each
month in turn for the by month analysis.  These kinds of analyses tend to get
quite complex so you have to keep on your toes, but so long as you understand
what's going on then the calculations are quite simple.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

I have just completed a CD-ROM of "Biostatistical Software" as advertised on
the Internet. If anybody is interested

Click here for more details

http://pages.prodigy.net/johnsonp12/biostat.html

Sincerely, Paul Johnson

The software includes:
i) Clinical trial software, ii) Model selection, iii) Quality control, iv)
Bootstrap, Monte Carlo, EM algorithm, and Box-Cox transformation, v)
Pharmaceutical and nonparametric, vi) Time series and wavelet analysis, vii)
Environmental and Ecological statistics, vii) Distance measure, degree of
agreement and various tests, viii) Statistical analysis package and a
Distributional library, ix) Randomization and Analysis-of-Mean Type tests,
and x) Regression, Estimation and sample size determination.

The CD-ROM costs $12.95 which includes shipping and handling to anywhere in
the world (so basically at cost).
I thought the subscribers of distance-sampling may be interested.

messages.subject: Fusing dedicated and opportunistic distance data
messages.subject_clean: Fusing dedicated and opportunistic distance data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I need some advice on handling and analysis of some distance sampling
data collected on a dedicated cetacean survey and the rest
opportunistically.

 I have two years of cetacean survey data collected off the
west coast of Scotland. During summer 1998, a five week double
platform cetacean survey, with eight observers, was conducted and
distance data recorded. However, after this initial survey all data
has been collected opportunistically from two vessels working in that
area. I had no say in either vessels route and I was the only
observer but I collected distance and angle data using reticle
binoculars and angleboard.

 I initially analysed the summers line transect survey data
and made an abundance estimate for the Atlantic white-sided dolphin.
However, I have additional white-sided sightings from my opportunistic
surveys in summer, autumn, and spring and was wondering:

1) whether it would be acceptable to combine these two data sets?

 If combining the datasets would be OK, then;

 2) Given there are not enough sightings to estimate seasonal
densities and since there is little evidence to suggest seasonal
movements of this species, I was thinking of pooling seasonal data to
get a combined estimate. I would assume that the detection function
of this species is constant for each season. Is this reasonable?

3) Most of the survey effort collected opportunistically outside
summer, is over the shelf/coastal (i.e. outside what's considered
white-sided dolphin habitat in this area). Therefore, should I only
incorporate "offshore" opportunbistic effort with the line transect
effort in the analysis?(perhaps define an offshore block?)

 4) I assume I would have to treat the sightings from the line
transect survey as a single platform survey through the elimination
of duplicate sights if they are to be combined with the opportunistic
data? There is also the problem of different numbers of observers and
I would have to assume the different vessels share a common detection
function.

 In short, I have two options - 1) analyse the line transect
survey data in isolation for a summer white-sided adundance estimate
or 2) fuse the data sets which would also increase the sample sizes
of other species and allow density estimates to be made. Can anyone
offer any advice on the best approach?

 Many thanks Kelly.
************************************************
Kelly MacLeod
Natural Resources Management Dept.
Natural Resources Institute
University of Greenwich
Chatham Maritime
Chatham
Kent
United Kingdom
ME4 4TB.
TEL: 01634 883090.
FAX: 01634 883517
E-MAIL: k.ma...@greenwich.ac.uk
